analysis.one_liner: Requires pathogen testing and safety limits for meat and poultry, with mandatory recalls and fines for unsafe products.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Agriculture Committee and its livestock subcommittee from April 1995 until Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal meat and poultry inspection law to target disease-causing bacteria rather than rely on visual inspection. It required plants to test for pathogens, set legal limits on contamination, treat contaminated meat as adulterated, give the Agriculture Secretary authority to order recalls, impose civil fines of up to $100,000 per day, protect whistleblowers, and create a system to trace contaminated animals back to their farm of origin. The bill's findings cite roughly 9,000 deaths and 6.5 to 80 million illnesses a year from foodborne disease, and $2 to $4 billion in annual medical and lost-wage costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially children, the elderly, and people with weakened immune systems who face the greatest risk from contaminated meat and poultry. The bill would have replaced the existing visual inspection system, which its findings said does not test for or limit bacteria, with a science-based system that tests products, sets contamination limits, and removes violating products from commerce. It would also have removed the USDA inspection seal when inspection no longer includes carcass-by-carcass review, so consumers are not misled about product safety.

how_it_helps.text: Requires meat and poultry plants to test products for human pathogens and report results to the government, with interim contamination limits set below the industry average and tightened every two years.
Treats products exceeding pathogen limits as adulterated and subject to condemnation, reprocessing, or destruction, and bars their sale or transport.
Gives the Agriculture Secretary authority to order recalls of unsafe or misbranded meat and poultry, with notice to consumers, and allows federal courts to order recalls directly.
Imposes civil penalties of up to $100,000 per day for violations and lets the Secretary withdraw inspection from plants that repeatedly fail to comply.
Protects plant employees who report violations or refuse to participate in them from harassment or discrimination, and opens plant food-safety records to public scrutiny.

Requires livestock and poultry to be identified so contaminated products can be traced back to their source, and directs federal agencies to build a nationwide foodborne-illness surveillance system with the CDC.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing plants, which would bear the cost of testing, hazard controls, recordkeeping, recalls, and potential fines; livestock and poultry producers, who would face animal identification and traceback record requirements; and grocery stores and restaurants, which would face handling and storage guidelines that become mandatory if most retailers do not comply voluntarily. Some of these costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meat and poultry processors, producers, retailers

drawbacks.text: Testing, hazard controls, recordkeeping, and traceback requirements would impose real compliance costs on processing plants, packinghouses, and livestock producers, with the heaviest relative burden on smaller operations, and some costs would be passed to shoppers through higher meat and poultry prices.

The bill extends federal authority into retail stores and restaurants through guidelines that automatically become mandatory regulations if the Secretary finds insufficient compliance, and it lets a State sue to enforce those rules.

The bill gives the Secretary discretion to compromise or remit civil penalties and to accept voluntary recalls in place of ordered ones, which an honest supporter would acknowledge weakens enforcement in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health stakes were large: the bill's own findings cite about 9,000 deaths and up to 80 million illnesses a year from foodborne illness, and $2 to $4 billion in annual medical and lost-wage costs from meat- and poultry-related illness. The compliance costs for industry and some price pressure on consumers are real but modest against that backdrop. The main design weakness is the bill's reliance on discretionary enforcement — penalty compromises and voluntary recalls — but it would still have created the first enforceable bacterial limits on meat and poultry, something the existing inspection system lacked.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1995 and sent to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to its livestock subcommittee; nothing further happened, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. George E. Brown Jr. of California, joined by Rep. Robert Torricelli, introduced the Family Food Protection Act of 1995 on April 6, 1995.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the day it was introduced, then referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy and Poultry the next day.
On May 1, 1995, executive comment was requested from the USDA; that was the last recorded action on the bill.
The bill had 23 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but the Agriculture Committee never held a markup and the House never voted on it before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processing plants and livestock producers were better off, because the bill's testing, traceback, recall, and penalty requirements never became law. The House Agriculture Committee, which never took the bill up, also avoided a fight over mandatory bacterial limits in an industry-heavy jurisdiction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and poultry processors and producers

for.name: Rep. George E. Brown Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require pathogen testing, bacterial limits, and recall authority for meat and poultry.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 6, 1995, sent it to its livestock subcommittee, and never reported it or scheduled any action on it.

against.name: Rep. Pat Roberts
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill during the 104th Congress.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory pathogen-testing and microbial-standard legislation of this kind during the 1990s food-safety debates.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 20 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of opposition never showed up in the record; the bill simply died in the Agriculture Committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required plants to test for pathogens, adopt hazard controls, keep records open to the public, accept government-ordered recalls, and pay civil fines of up to $100,000 per day. Contaminated products would have been condemned or reprocessed at the plant's expense. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers' interest in safer food.

The bill required animals presented for slaughter to be identified so contaminated meat could be traced back to the farm, with recordkeeping, inspections, and possible movement restrictions on animals from a contamination source. Producers would have borne identification and record costs.

Retail establishments would have faced voluntary federal guidelines for meat handling, temperature controls, and hygiene — but those guidelines would automatically become mandatory regulations if the Secretary found insufficient compliance, with States empowered to enforce them. The offset is that retailers sell food customers trust more when it is demonstrably safer.
